claims.text: The proposed framework decouples phonon and electron Boltzmann transport equations to predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivities separately.
The framework incorporates DFT-derived scattering rates, statistical atomic-scale disorder, impurity effects, and explicit anharmonic interactions.
The new method can accurately predict the total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
The new method will improve quantitative agreement with experiment by roughly 20–30% relative to existing models.
Electronic thermal transport predominates in HfNbTaTiZr below approximately 200 K.
The lattice contribution to thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr becomes increasingly significant above 300 K.
A temperature-dependent transport crossover will be observable when comparing impurity-free HfNbTaTiZr with material containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Chemical disorder, impurity-induced lattice distortions, and anharmonic lattice dynamics are structural mediators of heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Chemical disorder can scatter electrons more strongly than phonons in concentrated alloys.
Strong electron scattering and the resulting high electrical resistivity can suppress the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity.
Explicitly modeling impurity scattering and anharmonic phonon interactions will capture the asserted temperature dependence of lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Separately modeling electronic and lattice scattering will produce the asserted low-temperature electron-dominated and high-temperature phonon-enhanced behavior.
Predicted total thermal conductivities will agree within ±20–30% with experimental benchmarks for both ideal and 1 wt.% oxygen-modified samples.
Conventional analytical and simulation approaches generally assume ideal defect-free crystals or use simplified parameters such as Debye temperatures.
Conventional approaches typically conflate lattice and electronic heat transport.
The method is applicable from 50 to 1200 K and to oxygen concentrations up to approximately 1 wt.%.
Outside 50–1200 K or at impurity levels significantly above 1 wt.%, additional scattering mechanisms may invalidate the assumed decoupling.
The crossover temperature and conductivity improvement may vary by tens of kelvin or percentage points because of uncertainty in defect statistics and anharmonic parameters.
Failure to observe the asserted channel crossover, or a total-conductivity deviation greater than ±30%, would falsify the hypothesis.
